Prologue

The record, and the thing wrong with it

Two weeks ago we took the world record on Erdős minimum-overlap with a shared-tree league: two models, one PUCT search tree, each expanding the states the other found. Two arms differed only in whether the models also taught each other directly.

armwhat it is
QG-Shared-GRPOqwen3.5-27B + gemma-4-31B on one shared PUCT tree — the record
QG-Shared-GRPO+CEsame, plus a cross-entropy term: each model imitates the rival's rollouts that beat its own best

The two arms are one line of code apart. Everything up to the gradient is identical:

# ---- both arms: one tree, two policies -------------------------------
for step in 1..N:
    parents = puct_select(tree, k=16)              # 16 states by PUCT score
    for x in parents:
        Y_q = qwen.sample(prompt(x), n=32)         # 512 rollouts / model / step
        Y_g = gemma.sample(prompt(x), n=32)
        stage(x, Y_q, "qwen"); stage(x, Y_g, "gemma")

    # commit half/half: per parent, interleave each model's children by
    # value, best-first, capped at topk. Both models' discoveries become
    # everyone's parents next round — this is the whole sharing mechanism.
    balanced_commit(tree, staged, topk)

    for m in (qwen, gemma):                        # independent update each
        A_i  = r_i - mean(r_group)                 # GRPO, no std normalization
        L_m  = -sum_i A_i * ratio_i                # importance-weighted REINFORCE

        # ---- +CE arm only: frontier-gated cross-imitation ------------
        F_m     = max_i r(y^m_i)                   # my own best on this state
        imports = [y^rival_i  where  r(y^rival_i) > F_m]   # only what beats me
        q_i     = relu(r_i - F_m) / sum(relu(...)) # weight by margin over me
        L_ce    = -sum_i q_i * log pi_m(y^rival_i | x)     # re-rendered into MY format
        L_m     = L_m + 0.1 * L_ce                 # lambda = 0.1

        adam_step(L_m)

Then we found the problem. Spot preemption was silently resetting policy and optimizer weights without restoring them — the tree survived, the model did not. The record run had been restarting its policy from base at random intervals throughout training, and nobody chose that.

Consequence

The record stood, but no comparison in it was interpretable. Every arm had been taking an uncontrolled treatment. Everything below is the work of finding out what was actually true.

Question one

Is restart a feature or a bug?

If accidental restarts preceded our best results, maybe dropping the policy while keeping the tree is a real mechanism. Three arms, restart as the only variable.

armrestart policyresult
QG-Shared-GRPOnone — the clean control0.380862723716
…-Restart@Convergencefires when improvement stalls0.380864567696
…-Restart@8forced at step 8, once0.380870087219 died 11/20

What "convergence" meant, precisely

The trigger was derived from the four historical accidental restarts, not guessed. Let g_t be the improvement in best-so-far attributable to step t of the current life:

restart when the newest 3 consecutive steps all satisfy   gt < peak / 100
where peak = the second-largest prior gain of this life (once ≥3 observations)

Two deliberate details. The peak is the second-largest, because a fresh run's first family-discovery jump is ~10³× any steady step and would make every healthy step afterwards read as 100×-decayed — firing the trigger one step after the run's biggest success. And the 3-consecutive guard exists because the single-step version fired too eagerly under clean conditions: an earlier arm burned three restarts and finished last.

Restart itself means: drop LoRA weights and optimizer state, keep the tree. The discoveries are the asset; the policy is what has collapsed.

Verdict

Bug, not feature. The no-restart control won outright. The historical 50–90× recovery did not replicate at all. The sharpest form: the trigger correctly identified a stalled run, fired, and the restart still bought nothing — so the failure isn't trigger timing, it's that the intervention does not work under clean conditions.

Why the original observation was wrong: best-so-far is a running extremum over an append-only archive, so improvement follows every restart by construction. Measured that way the claim was unfalsifiable.

Question two

With the bug fixed, does the league still earn its cost?

The record came from two models sharing a tree. Rerun the base models alone, cleanly, and see what the second model actually contributed.

Verdict

One model was enough. Q-GRPO matches the shared-tree record. The record construction genuinely contains generations from both models — but only qwen was necessary. And weight sharing (+CE) actively costs, at equal budget with zero contamination on either side.

Question three

Why does the objective matter so much more for gemma?

Run both objectives on both models. The ordering doesn't just shift — it inverts, and the size of the gap changes by 8×.

Two variables are in play, and the diagnostics separate them cleanly.

Variable one — the model's inherent variance

Gemma is a low-variance generator. Its within-batch score spread is roughly half qwen's, its generations sit at a flat ~6,030 tokens, and it almost never breaks format. It produces consistent, similar answers. Qwen produces a mix.

armscore spreadformat failuresadvantage max
Q-GRPO0.091511.1%0.999
G-GRPO0.04721.0%0.789
Q-TTT-D0.061021.6%2.536
G-TTT-D0.02480.2%3.714

Both models start from similar average performance. But GRPO's advantage inherits the reward scale directly — so qwen's wider spread hands it a larger gradient for free, and gemma's tightness starves it. The ratio tracks variance, not quality: TTT-D buys qwen 2.5× its GRPO advantage, and gemma 4.7×.

One available fix that needs no new objective: raise gemma's sampling temperature to manufacture the spread it doesn't produce naturally.

The paradox in that table: qwen fails ten times more often, and wins

Gemma breaks format 1.0% of the time to qwen's 11.1%. It is also more correct (0.707 vs 0.565), better on mean construction quality, and better on worst-case construction quality. It loses anyway.

Discovery is a min-statistic, not a mean-statistic. The tree commits the best construction from each group of 32 and discards the other 31. Nothing about the average ever enters the archive, so a model competes on how far its tail reaches — not on how good its typical output is.

Seen that way, the format failures and the record are the same trait. Qwen's distribution is simply wider: its worst constructions are much worse (0.473 vs 0.428 mean-of-worst) and its best go lower. Breaking format 11% of the time is what taking bigger swings looks like from outside. And the failures cost little — 11% of 512 rollouts still leaves ~455 valid draws against gemma's ~507, and when you keep only the best of several hundred, a 10% difference in draw count is worth far less than a 2× difference in spread.

Note this is not an argument that failures are good. Raising qwen's learning rate reduced its failures and helped — two different levers on the same best-of-N objective. Within a model, more valid rollouts means more draws from the same distribution. Across models, the shape of the distribution dominates the number of draws. The learning rate bought draws; qwen's edge over gemma is shape.

It also means gemma's tightness hurts it twice over: narrower exploration in sample space, and weaker GRPO gradient signal, since mean-baseline advantage inherits that same small scale. Which is why the objective mattered so much more for gemma — the two findings share one cause.

Variable two — the objective function

GRPO (this codebase — no std normalization) Ai = ri − mean(r)
TTT-Discover β  solves  KL( softmax(β·r) ‖ uniform ) = ln 2   (bisection, per group)
wi = exp(β·ri) / Zi   Z = leave-one-out mean
Ai = wi − 1   ≥ −1 automatically

TTT-Discover's estimator is doing three jobs at once, and it's worth separating them:

  • β is a volume knob. It's solved per group so the attention distribution always carries exactly one bit — as selective as "keep half, drop half." When rewards are near-tied, β rises until the signal is full-size again. It is scale-invariant; GRPO is not.
  • The softmax weights the tail. Credit compounds toward the best sample rather than spreading linearly — it optimizes the best case, not the average.
  • The −1 floor caps the damage. Because w ≥ 0, no sample can score below −1 however badly it failed. Badness saturates.

Case study: what format failures do to each estimator

A typical group of 32 splits into a near-tied cluster of valid constructions and a tail of format failures. The measured scales are brutal: the total reward span is ~2.6 in every arm (valid vs failed), while the discovery signal — the score differences between valid constructions — is 0.025 to 0.09. The thing we don't need to learn is 30–100× louder than the thing we do.

Now trace one group through each estimator:

GRPO

Subtracting the mean gives a loud "don't fail format" signal and an almost-zero "this construction beats that one" signal. Standard deviation normalization doesn't help: σ is dominated by the failures, so dividing by it shrinks the valid cluster's differences further.

TTT-Discover

Failures get softmax weight ≈ e−β·2.6 ≈ 0, so they are invisible to the calibration. β ends up set by the valid cluster's own spread, amplifying exactly the differences that matter — and the −1 floor keeps the failures from exploding once β is large.

And the inversion falls out. Gemma has ten times fewer format failures than qwen (1.0% vs 11.1%), so its reward distribution is almost purely the tight valid cluster — which is precisely the regime where mean-baseline advantage collapses and β compensates hardest.

Two ways out

Take bigger steps

If the gradient magnitude decays monotonically over training, raise the learning rate rather than reshaping the objective.

Give GRPO the volume knob

Keep linear "improvement over the mean" credit, borrow TTD's calibration:

Ai = clamp( β·(ri − center), min = −1 )
center = Σ softmax(β·r)i · ri

The centering matters as much as the scaling. Using the plain arithmetic mean, the failures drag it ~0.75 below the valid cluster, so β·(r − mean) hands every valid sample a huge near-identical positive advantage — and no top-clip can fix that without erasing the differences β exists to resolve. The softmax-weighted center sits inside the cluster, where the failures have no vote.

Meta-question

TTT-Discover's central claim is that reinforcing the tail of the reward distribution is the best strategy. Combined with a PUCT tree, that may be redundant. We already commit the top children of each parent, and a construction that improved gets selected as a parent next round — so the winning behavior is in context on the very next step. Why spend gradient memorizing what the tree is about to hand back for free? That is an argument for GRPO's linear credit: reinforce general improvement, and let the search remember the maximum.

Question four

If the gradient shrinks, just take bigger steps

The cheapest version of the fix. Same objective, same batch, same budget, same tree — move only the LoRA learning rate off the inherited 4e-5 default.

Result

Q-GRPO-1.5e-4 = 0.380859354888 — the best verified C₅ in the program, and it improved on 14 of 14 banked steps without once plateauing. The mechanism is measurable: correctness (the fraction of rollouts producing a valid, scoreable construction) rose from 0.565 to 0.780 on average and 0.756 → 0.947 by the end — about 307 → 460 usable rollouts per 512-rollout step. More valid children mean better parents, which compounds.

An honest wrinkle, and a hint at what comes next: the higher LR is behind at steps 2–5 and only overtakes at step 6 — the gain compounds rather than arriving. And by its final third it was running with advantage max 0.448, below even gemma-GRPO's, grinding out its last improvements on a nearly flat gradient. The winning arm spent its endgame in exactly the regime where β-scaling should help most. So the two fixes ought to compose.

Read as a ladder at fixed learning rate, each rung changing exactly one thing: GRPO → +β scale/center/floor → full exponential. Wherever the score moves, that rung names the mechanism.

The next hypothesis

The best model is not static

Single-agent work tells us the right objective and learning rate. But the original multi-agent intuition survives all of it, for a reason visible in the data: which model is best depends on the problem.

So the question is not "which model" but: when a model converges, does switching to a different one on the same tree keep the search moving?

The simple test: take qwen's converged state and put fresh gemma weights on top of its tree.

Meta-optimization over models

If refining a model's solution set eventually saturates, the natural move is to keep going with a different model — a greedy tree search where each node is a full single-agent training run, and the branching factor is the model roster.

State reuse — what seeds the next round

A. Top-K states from the winning model only.
B. Top-K pooled across all models from the previous round.

Policy reuse — what the next round starts from

1. Fresh model weights each round.
2. Continue the previous round's weights.

Four configurations, run to depth 5 over Muse-Glimmer, gemma and qwen at 1.5e-4 with plain GRPO — deliberately the simplest objective, so the meta-search is measured against a known single-agent recipe rather than a moving one.

Caveat

The tree-swap result above is uncontrolled. Its matching qwen-on-qwen control was killed for grading contamination, so we cannot yet separate "the tree carried the discovery" from "gemma is simply different." A clean control is the prerequisite for reading anything into the meta-optimization.

Where this goes

Experimental plan

  • Finish refining the optimal single-agent recipe — objective, learning rate, and whether the β fixes compose with the LR fix.
  • Apply that recipe to meta-optimization over models, with a clean control for the tree-vs-model split.
  • Extend to multiple problems — Erdős, JSSP and ac_inequalities already disagree about which model is best.
  • Extend to agents.

Standing caveats

  • Single seed per arm. Contrasts inside roughly 2× are screening results. The LR win is large and mechanistically explained, but it is one run.
  • Cross-objective comparisons carry a bundle. GRPO runs 16×32 and TTT-Discover 8×32 by design, so "GRPO vs TTD" is each method as canonically configured — not a clean objective ablation. Only the hybrid arms share GRPO's exact batch shape.
  • How the best-so-far curves are built. The logged pool metric is the best in the sampler's current pool, not a running extremum, so it can rise when the pool drops a state. The curves plot a true running minimum, and ignore any per-step reading better than the run's own verified final tree value.
  • The fleet is capacity-bound. Most queued arms above are waiting on spot capacity in us-east5-a rather than running.

Every C₅ in this document was recomputed from its stored construction — verifying that sum(h) = n/2 holds exactly and that the recomputed score matches to float round-trip — after we found that the grader had been returning the score a program claimed rather than the one it achieved. That bug did not just corrupt numbers; in one arm it froze the search for seven steps by planting an unreachable best. The strict-scoring rerun of that arm improved on 13 of 14 steps instead of 8.
